blogs.title: Video as Veracity: The Body Camera in Fourth Amendment Suppression Hearings
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Seventh Circuit's reliance on body-worn camera footage to resolve Fourth Amendment factual disputes. The opinion explicitly cites United States v. Norville and Scott v. Harris, suggesting a paradigm shift where video evidence may render oral testimony or ambiguous accounts in suppression hearings practically irrelevant. We'll discuss the procedural implications of this evidentiary weight and whether it improves the reliability of consent findings compared to traditional affidavit-based hearings.

blogs.title: The 'Welfare Check' Exception: How Domestic Violence Calls Expand Police Search Authority
blogs.description: Focusing on the specific context of responding to domestic violence calls, this post examines how consent to enter a home is defined when officer safety and child welfare are at stake. We will explore the 'scope of consent' doctrine as applied when one suspect's threat implicates third-party victims, and analyze where the line is drawn between a limited welfare sweep and a general warrantless search for property, particularly firearms.

blogs.title: The Semiotics of Consent: Why 'Need' Didn't Silence the Fourth Amendment
blogs.description: This post dissects the voluntariness of consent inquiry, specifically analyzing the district court's and appellate court's rejection of Coleman's claim that Officer Kizer's use of the word 'need' constituted coercion. Drawing on the totality of the circumstances test and the Bumper inquiry, we discuss how courts weigh language choice against officer demeanor and the victim's demonstrated capacity to refuse, highlighting the nuance in policing where concern is legally distinct from coercion.
